note: Raw findings as each reader returned them. A finding is the reader's claim, not a verified fact; see 2026-11-21-mark-grounding-review.md for what the lead verified.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, mostly not Jewish — Mark explains Jewish customs and translates every Aramaic phrase
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenFor ("Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference...") and bookBriefing.language.readerSignal ("does not identify a city or prove that every reader was Gentile") and bookBriefing.language.writtenIn ("in several places, translated for the reader")
findings.problem: The audience field drops the briefing's uncertainty, upgrades "probably including Gentiles" to "mostly not Jewish," and overstates "in several places" as "every Aramaic phrase."

findings.guideText: In ordinary Greek, the announcement of a victory or the arrival of a ruler — a herald's word, not originally a religious one.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.form and bookBriefing.language (contain no Greek lexical claim about "Gospel" as a herald's word for a victory or ruler's arrival)
findings.problem: This Greek linguistic claim about the ordinary meaning of "Gospel" is not supported by the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: Their authority came from citing tradition — which is exactly the contrast being drawn in verse 22.
findings.evidence: 1:22 ("for he taught them as having authority, and not as the scribes") and bookBriefing.cast ("Religious teachers and legal experts")
findings.problem: Neither verse 22 nor the book briefing states that the scribes' authority came from citing tradition or that this is the exact contrast being drawn.

findings.guideText: John in the desert, quoting Isaiah, pointing past himself
findings.evidence: 1:2-3 ("As it is written in the prophets...") and 1:4 ("John came baptizing in the wilderness...")
findings.problem: The hosted text attributes the quotation in verses 2-3 to the narrator citing "the prophets," not to John quoting Isaiah.

findings.guideText: Read from inside the book: the crowds already treat him as a miracle-worker and would happily make him a rebel king, and once that label sticks the actual mission — dying — becomes impossible to explain.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.snags[1] ("Other readers treat the secrecy as Mark's storytelling device, so this remains an interpretation rather than a settled fact.")
findings.problem: The answer presents one explanation of the messianic secret as settled without noting that readers differ and treat it as an interpretation.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, mostly not Jewish — Mark explains Jewish customs and translates every Aramaic phrase
findings.evidence: Briefing facts.writtenFor: “Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference”
findings.problem: The guide drops the briefing’s “likely/probably” uncertainty and turns “probably including Gentiles” into “mostly not Jewish.”

findings.guideText: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s
findings.evidence: Briefing facts.writtenWhen: “Most scholarship places it from the mid-AD 60s to shortly after 70, though earlier dates are defended.”
findings.problem: The guide widens the main scholarly range back into the AD 50s without preserving the briefing’s distinction between the majority range and earlier defended dates.

findings.guideText: In ordinary Greek, the announcement of a victory or the arrival of a ruler — a herald's word, not originally a religious one.
findings.evidence: Briefing language.writtenIn: “Koine Greek”; its supplied Greek features cover εὐθύς, καί, and the historical present, with no claim about the ordinary Greek meaning of the word behind “Good News.”
findings.problem: This Greek lexical-history claim is stated as fact but is not supported by the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: To turn around and go a different way. It can carry regret, but the core of the word is change of direction, not feeling bad.
findings.evidence: Mark 1:15: “Repent, and believe in the Good News.” Briefing language features supply no Greek or Hebrew definition of “repent.”
findings.problem: The guide states a word-core linguistic claim about “repent” that neither the hosted chapter nor the briefing supports.

findings.guideText: John in the desert, quoting Isaiah, pointing past himself
findings.evidence: Mark 1:2: “As it is written in the prophets, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face…’”; TSK links 1:2 to MAL 3:1 and 1:3 to ISA 40:3-5
findings.problem: The opening quotation is presented in the hosted text as from “the prophets” and is composite, not simply a quotation of Isaiah.

findings.guideText: Not a place you go when you die, and not a political state. It means God's rule breaking into the present — the world starting to run the way it was meant to. 'At hand' means close enough to touch.
findings.evidence: Mark 1:15: “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.” Briefing whereYouAre: Jewish hopes “take several forms — political, national, and religious — rather than one single expectation.”
findings.problem: The guide gives one contested definition of the kingdom as settled fact and excludes political expectation despite the briefing’s diversity of hopes.

findings.guideText: the crowds already treat him as a miracle-worker and would happily make him a rebel king, and once that label sticks the actual mission — dying — becomes impossible to explain
findings.evidence: Briefing snags on secrecy: “Other readers treat the secrecy as Mark's storytelling device, so this remains an interpretation rather than a settled fact.”
findings.problem: The guide presents one reading of the messianic secret, plus an invented “rebel king” motive, as the explanation without naming the briefing’s alternative reading.

findings.guideText: Non-Jewish readers who need the customs explained — note how the Sabbath dispute is spelled out
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenFor ("Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference: the book explains Jewish handwashing customs (7:3-4) and translates the Aramaic phrases it quotes.") and bookBriefing.language.readerSignal ("by itself it does not identify a city or prove that every reader was Gentile.")
findings.problem: The guide drops the briefing's uncertainty by stating flatly that the audience is non-Jewish readers, and wrongly cites the Sabbath dispute in Mark 2 as an explained custom rather than the handwashing customs in 7:3-4.

findings.guideText: A Galilean village house had a flat roof of wooden beams packed with branches and dried mud, reached by an outside stair, used for sleeping and drying grain.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:4 ("they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on.") and bookBriefing (no architectural details of Galilean roofs)
findings.problem: The guide states specific archaeological claims about Galilean house construction and roof use as fact without support from the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: Tax collectors in Galilee worked for Herod Antipas and, behind him, Rome — collaborating with the occupying power against their own people — and the system let them keep whatever they squeezed above the quota.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:14 ("Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax office") and bookBriefing.whereYouAre ("Galilee is ruled by Herod Antipas under Roman power.")
findings.problem: Neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supports the historical claims about how Galilean tax-collection quotas and excess profits operated.

findings.guideText: Some take the Greek phrase as 'in the passage about Abiathar,' pointing to the section of scripture rather than the moment.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:26 ("at the time of Abiathar the high priest") and bookBriefing.language (no Greek analysis of 2:26)
findings.problem: The guide makes a linguistic claim about the Greek phrasing of Mark 2:26 that is not present in the supplied book briefing.

findings.guideText: In everyday Aramaic the phrase can just mean 'a human being,'
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.snags[4] ("\"Son of Man\" sounds like it means \"just a human.\"") and bookBriefing.language.spokenWorld
findings.problem: The guide makes an Aramaic linguistic claim about the phrase "Son of Man" that is not supported by the supplied book briefing.

findings.guideText: The phrase lets him make an enormous claim without ever using the word king — useful in a province where claiming kingship got you executed.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.snags[4] ("the phrase can carry more than one force: a human being, a suffering figure, or the Daniel 7:13 figure given authority by God. ... not every use has to mean exactly the same thing.")
findings.problem: The guide treats every use of "Son of Man" as a calculated royal claim and supplies an ungrounded motive, flattening the range of meanings preserved in the book briefing.

findings.guideText: Five short confrontations, back to back.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:1-28 and guide outline (verses 1-12, 13-17, 18-22, 23-28)
findings.problem: Mark 2 contains four confrontations (2:1-12, 2:15-17, 2:18-22, and 2:23-28), not five, as Levi's call in 2:13-14 involves no confrontation.

findings.guideText: Non-Jewish readers who need the customs explained — note how the Sabbath dispute is spelled out
findings.evidence: Book briefing, writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference: the book explains Jewish handwashing customs (7:3-4) and translates the Aramaic phrases it quotes."
findings.problem: The guide turns a likely, inferred audience into settled non-Jewish readership and substitutes an explanatory example the briefing does not give.

findings.guideText: Capernaum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, and the grain fields around it
findings.evidence: Mark 2:1 names Capernaum, 2:13 says "by the seaside," and 2:23 mentions grain fields; neither the chapter nor the briefing calls Capernaum a fishing town or names the Sea of Galilee.
findings.problem: The setting adds geographic and occupational details that the supplied sources do not state.

findings.guideText: Under the law it was a capital charge, which is why the accusation here is not a small one.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:7: "Why does this man speak blasphemies like that? Who can forgive sins but God alone?" The chapter and briefing do not state the legal penalty for blasphemy.
findings.problem: The capital-charge claim is an unsupported legal-historical detail.

findings.guideText: A principle for reading every rule in the book — the rule exists to serve people, not the reverse.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:27: "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."
findings.problem: The guide expands a saying specifically about the Sabbath into a principle governing every rule.

findings.guideText: A Galilean village house had a flat roof of wooden beams packed with branches and dried mud, reached by an outside stair, used for sleeping and drying grain. You could dig through it and patch it afterward.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:4: "they removed the roof where he was. When they had broken it up, they let down the mat that the paralytic was lying on."
findings.problem: The chapter and briefing provide none of these architectural or household-use details.

findings.guideText: the system let them keep whatever they squeezed above the quota
findings.evidence: Mark 2:14 says Levi was "sitting at the tax office"; the briefing says only that Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas under Roman power.
findings.problem: The quota-and-overcollection system is stated as fact without support in the chapter or briefing.

findings.guideText: Beyond the one day the law required, devout groups fasted regularly by choice, and it marked you as serious.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:18: "John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting"; neither the chapter nor the briefing specifies a legally required fast day or the groups’ fasting frequency.
findings.problem: The legal requirement and regular devotional practice are unsupported historical claims stated as fact.

findings.guideText: The phrase lets him make an enormous claim without ever using the word king — useful in a province where claiming kingship got you executed.
findings.evidence: Mark 2:10 and 2:28 use "Son of Man" but mention neither kingship nor execution; the briefing says the phrase can carry more than one force and that Mark makes the Daniel connection explicit at 13:26 and 14:62.
findings.problem: The guide invents a strategic motive and adds an unsupported historical claim about execution for claiming kingship.

findings.guideText: Non-Jewish readers — note that Mark stops to translate the nickname 'Boanerges' in verse 17
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenFor ("Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference...") and bookBriefing.language.readerSignal ("by itself it does not identify a city or prove that every reader was Gentile.")
findings.problem: The guide states flatly that the audience was "Non-Jewish readers," dropping the book briefing's explicit uncertainty that Gentile readership is an inference and not proven for every reader.

findings.guideText: The Greek phrase covers his relatives or close associates, and the verb for what they came to do is forceful — to seize or take charge of him.
findings.evidence: Mark 3:21 ("When his friends heard it, they went out to seize him; for they said, “He is insane.”") and bookBriefing.language (contains no discussion of the Greek phrase or verb in 3:21)
findings.problem: The guide makes claims about the underlying Greek phrase and verb in Mark 3:21 that are not supported by the hosted chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: Verse 21 says his family thought he was insane.
findings.evidence: Mark 3:21 ("When his friends heard it, they went out to seize him; for they said, “He is insane.”")
findings.problem: The guide states that verse 21 says Jesus's "family" thought he was insane, whereas the hosted World English Bible text of 3:21 says "his friends."

findings.guideText: Non-Jewish readers — note that Mark stops to translate the nickname 'Boanerges' in verse 17
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference"; readerSignal adds it does not prove every reader was Gentile.
findings.problem: The guide turns a likely, mixed-audience inference into exclusively non-Jewish readers and drops the briefing's uncertainty.

findings.guideText: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenWhen: "Most scholarship places it from the mid-AD 60s to shortly after 70, though earlier dates are defended."
findings.problem: The range presents the 50s as equally in play without noting that most scholarship begins in the mid-60s and earlier dates are the defended minority.

findings.guideText: a hint at their temperament
findings.evidence: 3:17 says only that James and John were called "Boanerges, which means, Sons of Thunder"; neither the verse nor the briefing assigns a temperament.
findings.problem: A character trait is inferred from the nickname and stated as its meaning-bearing hint without textual support.

findings.guideText: It marks intense devotion to the law and, in this period, sympathy with armed resistance to Rome — which makes the presence of a tax collector in the same group of twelve remarkable.
findings.evidence: 3:18 lists only "Simon the Zealot" among the names, with no definition of Zealot and no identification of Matthew as a tax collector in this chapter; the briefing provides neither claim.
findings.problem: The armed-resistance definition and the tax-collector contrast are historical claims the chapter and briefing do not support.

findings.guideText: People come from five regions; the unclean spirits keep announcing him and keep getting silenced
findings.evidence: 3:7-8 lists Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumaea, beyond the Jordan, and those from around Tyre and Sidon.
findings.problem: The hosted text names more than five places or regions.

findings.guideText: Healing counted as work, and the accepted position allowed it on the Sabbath only when a life was in danger.
findings.evidence: 3:2 says only that they watched whether he would heal on the Sabbath so they might accuse him; 3:4 asks whether it is lawful to do good or harm, save life or kill. Neither the chapter nor the briefing states an accepted life-in-danger-only rule.
findings.problem: A specific Sabbath-law position is stated as fact without support in the chapter or briefing.

findings.guideText: The Pharisees were a devout renewal movement with no love for Herod's court. These two groups had little reason to cooperate on anything.
findings.evidence: 3:6 says only that "The Pharisees went out, and immediately conspired with the Herodians against him"; the briefing cast describes Pharisees and scribes as religious teachers and legal experts, with no claim about their relation to Herod's court.
findings.problem: The alleged mutual hostility that makes the alliance remarkable is not in the chapter or briefing.

findings.guideText: Almost certainly. Israel was founded as twelve tribes, and by this period most of them had long since been scattered. Appointing exactly twelve men reads as a deliberate claim: this is Israel being restarted.
findings.evidence: 3:14 says only "He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach"; the chapter gives no tribal explanation for the number.
findings.problem: The guide claims near-certainty for a symbolic reading the text does not spell out, without naming that readers may read the number differently.

findings.guideText: The Greek phrase covers his relatives or close associates, and the verb for what they came to do is forceful — to seize or take charge of him.
findings.evidence: Hosted 3:21 reads "When his friends heard it, they went out to seize him"; the briefing's language section gives no Greek analysis of 3:21.
findings.problem: A Greek lexical claim is made that neither the hosted translation nor the supplied briefing supports.

findings.guideText: It is the settled decision to name good as evil, which by its nature will not seek forgiveness. Readers across traditions have generally observed that anxiety about having committed it is itself evidence to the contrary.
findings.evidence: 3:28-30 attaches the warning to blasphemy against the Holy Spirit "because they said, 'He has an unclean spirit'"; nothing in the chapter or briefing defines it as a settled decision or offers the anxiety test.
findings.problem: The guide preaches a definitive definition and pastoral reassurance beyond what the verses and briefing give.

findings.guideText: Worth noting that Mark shows the same brothers unconvinced here, and that James, one of them, later leads the church in Jerusalem.
findings.evidence: 3:31-32 names only "His mother and his brothers" and "your mother, your brothers, and your sisters"; no brother is named James in this chapter and no later Jerusalem leadership appears in the chapter or briefing.
findings.problem: The identity of a named brother and his later church role are imported without support from this chapter or the briefing.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, not familiar with Galilean farming or the lake
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference: the book explains Jewish handwashing customs (7:3-4) and translates the Aramaic phrases it quotes."
findings.problem: The audience field drops the briefing's "Likely" uncertainty and adds an unsupported claim that readers were unfamiliar with Galilean farming or the lake.

findings.guideText: The verb used for the wind in verse 39 is the same one used to silence the unclean spirit in 1:25 — the storm is addressed the way a hostile power is addressed.
findings.evidence: Mark 4:39 (WEB) uses "rebuked", while Mark 1:25 is outside the chapter and the book briefing makes no claim about a shared verb between 1:25 and 4:39.
findings.problem: This asserts a lexical identity between Mark 4:39 and Mark 1:25 that is not supported by the hosted chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: The verb 'rebuked' is the same one used on demons in chapter 1 — Mark is not describing a weather forecast.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.snags cites 1:25 and 1:34 only for secrecy commands, and neither the chapter 4 text nor the book briefing mentions a shared Greek verb in chapter 1.
findings.problem: This makes a cross-chapter linguistic claim about the Greek verb in Mark 1 that neither the hosted chapter text nor the book briefing supports.

findings.guideText: Second, the Aramaic behind 'that' can carry the sense of result rather than purpose: this is what happens, not this is the aim.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language.writtenIn: "Koine Greek. Mark's narrative and its earliest surviving manuscripts are Greek." and bookBriefing.language.textualHistory: "Every recoverable form of Mark is a Greek book."
findings.problem: This asserts an Aramaic linguistic claim behind the wording of Mark 4:12 that is not supported by the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: 'smaller than all the seeds on earth'
findings.evidence: Mark 4:31 (WEB): "though it is less than all the seeds that are on the earth"
findings.problem: The quoted phrase alters the hosted World English Bible wording ("less than all the seeds that are on the earth") to "smaller than all the seeds on earth."

findings.guideText: Mark uses a strong phrase — they feared a great fear —
findings.evidence: Mark 4:41 (WEB): "They were greatly afraid"
findings.problem: The guide cites a literalistic rendering of the underlying Greek ("they feared a great fear") that is neither in the hosted World English Bible text nor in the book briefing.

findings.guideText: he stops it with two words
findings.evidence: Mark 4:39 (WEB): “Peace! Be still!”
findings.problem: The summary says Jesus stops the storm with two words, whereas the hosted World English Bible text has three words (“Peace! Be still!”).

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, not familiar with Galilean farming or the lake
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference"
findings.problem: The guide turns the briefing's hedged inference into a definite claim and adds unfamiliarity with farming and the lake that the briefing does not state.

findings.guideText: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenWhen: "Most scholarship places it from the mid-AD 60s to shortly after 70, though earlier dates are defended."
findings.problem: The guide replaces the briefing's weighted range with a broader 50s-70s range and drops the distinction between the majority range and earlier defended dates.

findings.guideText: The shore of the Sea of Galilee — a lake about 13 miles long, ringed by hills that funnel sudden violent winds down onto the water
findings.evidence: Mark 4:1: "he entered into a boat in the sea and sat down. All the multitude were on the land by the sea."
findings.problem: Neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supports the lake's stated size or the claim that surrounding hills funnel violent winds onto it.

findings.guideText: The verb used for the wind in verse 39 is the same one used to silence the unclean spirit in 1:25
findings.evidence: Mark 4:39: "He awoke and rebuked the wind"; the briefing's language features and examples contain no such verb comparison with Mark 1:25.
findings.problem: The glossary repeats a Greek lexical-identity claim that neither the hosted chapter nor the book briefing supports.

findings.guideText: A freshwater lake roughly 13 miles by 7, about 700 feet below sea level, notorious for sudden squalls funnelled down from the surrounding hills.
findings.evidence: Mark 4:1 and 4:37 mention the sea and a "big wind storm" but provide no dimensions, elevation, or funneling explanation, and the briefing supplies none.
findings.problem: The glossary states specific geographical facts about the lake that are unsupported by the grounding bundle.

findings.guideText: The verb 'rebuked' is the same one used on demons in chapter 1
findings.evidence: Mark 4:39: "He awoke and rebuked the wind"; the briefing's language section contains no claim identifying this Greek verb with the verb used in Mark 1.
findings.problem: This Greek lexical-identity claim is not supplied by the chapter text or the book briefing and should have been left out under the grounding rules.

findings.evidence: Mark 4:33-34: "With many such parables he spoke the word to them... Without a parable he didn’t speak to them"; the storm narrative begins at 4:35.
findings.problem: The outline labels verses 33-41 as the storm section even though verses 33-34 still concern Jesus speaking in parables.

findings.guideText: Seed was broadcast by hand across the whole field first and ploughed in afterward, so some inevitably landed on the footpath running through it, on the thin soil over bedrock, and at the weedy edges.
findings.evidence: Mark 4:3-7 describes seed falling by the road, on rocky ground, and among thorns, but gives no account of broadcast-then-ploughing practice.
findings.problem: The specific ancient sowing method is stated as historical fact without support from the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: the Aramaic behind 'that' can carry the sense of result rather than purpose
findings.evidence: Briefing textualHistory: "Every recoverable form of Mark is a Greek book" and "recovering any earlier Aramaic form requires a method rather than simply reversing a translation."
findings.problem: The guide asserts an Aramaic linguistic explanation behind Mark's Greek wording that the briefing does not supply and that its transmission discussion cautions against deriving this way.

findings.guideText: A good harvest in that agriculture returned something in the range of tenfold.
findings.evidence: Mark 4:8 and 4:20 give only the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold yields; neither the chapter nor the briefing gives a normal tenfold harvest benchmark.
findings.problem: The comparative historical harvest figure is stated as fact without support in the grounding bundle.

findings.guideText: The phrase was a proverbial expression for something tiny, the way we say a grain of sand, and it is comparing garden seeds a Galilean farmer would actually sow.
findings.evidence: Mark 4:31: "though it is less than all the seeds that are on the earth"; neither the chapter nor the briefing identifies the phrase as a proverb restricted to garden seeds.
findings.problem: The guide presents a specific linguistic and historical explanation of the mustard-seed phrase that the grounding bundle does not support.

findings.guideText: The Sea of Galilee sits about 700 feet below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines that channel cold air down onto warm water. Violent squalls arrive with very little warning and can drop again just as quickly.
findings.evidence: Mark 4:37: "A big wind storm arose, and the waves beat into the boat"; neither the chapter nor the briefing gives the lake's elevation, topography, or squall mechanism.
findings.problem: These geographical and meteorological details are stated as fact without support from the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: Mark uses a strong phrase — they feared a great fear
findings.evidence: Mark 4:41 in the hosted text: "They were greatly afraid"; the briefing's language section supplies no literal Greek rendering "they feared a great fear" for this verse.
findings.problem: This underlying Greek phrasing claim is not in the supplied briefing and should have been left out under the grounding rules.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea — Mark translates the Aramaic 'Talitha cumi' and explains nothing about pigs, assuming his readers already keep them
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.facts.writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference: the book explains Jewish handwashing customs (7:3-4) and translates the Aramaic phrases it quotes."
findings.problem: The audience field drops the briefing's uncertainty and adds an unsupported claim that Mark assumes his readers keep pigs.

findings.guideText: Notice he is not Jewish — the silence rule does not apply out here.
findings.evidence: Mark 5:1, 5:19-20 (names the country of the Gadarenes and Decapolis without stating the man's ethnicity)
findings.problem: The note states as fact that the healed man is not Jewish even though the chapter text only identifies the region and not his ethnicity.

findings.guideText: It is a real and deliberate reversal, and the geography explains it. In Jewish Galilee, the title 'Messiah' carried the expectation of a warrior king, so publicity was dangerous. In the Decapolis, ten Gentile cities where nobody was waiting for a Jewish deliverer, that risk was absent.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.snags[1]: "Other readers treat the secrecy as Mark's storytelling device, so this remains an interpretation rather than a settled fact." and bookBriefing.whereYouAre: "Jewish hopes for God's deliverance take several forms — political, national, and religious — rather than one single expectation."
findings.problem: The answer presents one interpretation of the secrecy motif and Jewish messianic expectation as settled fact when the briefing marks both as unsettled or varied.

findings.guideText: Keeping the sound is the mark of a memory passed down by people who heard it. Translating it is the mark of a writer whose readers do not speak that language. Both things are true at once, and together they tell you something about how this book came to be.
findings.evidence: bookBriefing.sources (delgado-socioling): "treats the preserved forms as social and literary choices rather than accidental leftovers."
findings.problem: The answer states as settled fact that preserving Aramaic phrases is a mark of eyewitness memory, whereas the briefing notes they can also be read as social and literary choices.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea — Mark translates the Aramaic 'Talitha cumi' and explains nothing about pigs, assuming his readers already keep them
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference: the book explains Jewish handwashing customs (7:3-4) and translates the Aramaic phrases it quotes."
findings.problem: The guide states the audience as certain and adds an unsupported pig-keeping inference that the briefing does not make.

findings.guideText: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenWhen: "Most scholarship places it from the mid-AD 60s to shortly after 70, though earlier dates are defended."
findings.problem: The guide widens and flattens the briefing's dating position and drops its stated scholarly centre.

findings.guideText: Narrative, including Mark's signature sandwich — the woman's story is set inside the girl's
findings.evidence: Briefing form.name: "Gospel — an ancient life-of-a-person written to persuade, not a diary or a news report"
findings.problem: The guide replaces the briefing's Gospel/ancient-biography form with generic narrative.

findings.guideText: Notice he is not Jewish — the silence rule does not apply out here.
findings.evidence: Mark 5:19-20 says the man was sent home and proclaimed in Decapolis; neither verse states the man's ethnicity or a geographic limit to a silence rule.
findings.problem: The guide asserts the man's ethnicity and the reason for the instruction without textual or briefing support.

findings.guideText: 'Daughter' is the only time he calls anyone that.
findings.evidence: Mark 5:34: "Daughter, your faith has made you well." No briefing line supports a whole-Mark uniqueness claim.
findings.problem: A book-wide uniqueness claim is stated as fact from a single chapter instance.

findings.guideText: A legion was a Roman army unit of several thousand men.
findings.evidence: Mark 5:9: "My name is Legion, for we are many."
findings.problem: The verse supports number in general, not the specific Roman-unit size claimed as fact.

findings.guideText: It is the kind of specific, unnecessary thing that tends to come from someone who was in the room.
findings.evidence: Briefing source papias: Mark "never heard Jesus himself"; language caution also warns style is "not proof that the author was remembering an eyewitness scene."
findings.problem: The guide implies eyewitness origin for a narrative detail, contrary to the briefing's caution.

findings.guideText: It is a real and deliberate reversal, and the geography explains it.
findings.evidence: Briefing snag on secrecy: "Other readers treat the secrecy as Mark's storytelling device, so this remains an interpretation rather than a settled fact."
findings.problem: The guide presents one contested explanation of Mark's secrecy pattern as settled geography-based fact.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea; Mark keeps the Aramaic 'Abba' and explains the Passover timing
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: “Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference”

findings.guideText: Passion narrative, the oldest continuous block of gospel tradition, with Mark's sandwich technique framing the trial and the denial

findings.problem: The field replaces the briefing’s literary form and adds an unsupported claim that this is the oldest continuous block of gospel tradition.

findings.guideText: Bethany, an upper room in Jerusalem, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and the high priest's house — all within one night
findings.evidence: 14:1 “It was now two days before the Passover”; 14:12 “On the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover”
findings.problem: The chapter spans from two days before Passover to the Passover night, so the events are not all within one night.

findings.guideText: wherever this Good News may be preached throughout the whole world, that which this woman has done will also be spoken of for a memorial of her.

findings.problem: The quotation silently omits the opening words of the hosted verse without an ellipsis.

findings.guideText: Denial — inner half resolved
findings.evidence: 14:54 Peter is placed in the courtyard before the trial; 14:66 returns to Peter below; briefing form describes “Jesus on trial upstairs while Peter denies him in the courtyard below (14:53-72)”
findings.problem: Peter’s denial is the outer frame of the sandwich and the trial is the inner scene, not the reverse.

findings.guideText: Three hundred denarii is close to a year's wages for a labourer. Nard was imported from the Himalayan region, and the jar was sealed — breaking it meant it could not be resealed or used sparingly.
findings.evidence: 14:3 “an alabaster jar of ointment of pure nard—very costly. She broke the jar”; 14:5 “more than three hundred denarii”
findings.problem: Neither the chapter text nor the briefing supports the wage comparison, Himalayan origin, or sealed-jar claims.

findings.guideText: a phrase that also echoes the divine name in Exodus 3:14
findings.evidence: 14:62 “I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky”
findings.problem: Neither the chapter text nor the briefing supports the linguistic claim that this “I am” echoes the divine name in Exodus 3:14.

findings.guideText: The high priest tears his clothes, the prescribed response to hearing blasphemy, and no further witnesses are needed.
findings.evidence: 14:63 “The high priest tore his clothes and said, “What further need have we of witnesses?””
findings.problem: The verse reports the tearing but neither it nor the briefing supports the claim that this was the prescribed response to blasphemy.

findings.guideText: Pouring oil on the head is how kings were anointed in Israel — the word Messiah means anointed one.
findings.evidence: 14:3 “poured it over his head”; 14:8 “She has anointed my body beforehand for the burying”
findings.problem: The chapter and briefing do not support the historical claim that this head-pouring reproduces Israel’s royal anointing practice.

findings.guideText: Because carrying water was women's work, so a man doing it stood out in a crowded festival city.
findings.evidence: 14:13 “a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you”
findings.problem: The social-history claim that water-carrying was women’s work is stated as fact but is supported by neither the chapter text nor the briefing.

findings.guideText: What every side agrees on: he said it at a Passover meal, where the bread and herbs were already understood to make a past deliverance present to the people eating, and he told them to keep doing it.
findings.evidence: 14:22 “Take, eat. This is my body”; 14:24 “This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many”
findings.problem: Mark 14 contains no instruction to keep repeating the meal; that command belongs to other accounts and is imported here.

findings.guideText: It is the ordinary Aramaic word a child used for their father — warm and familial, though not baby talk as is sometimes claimed.
findings.evidence: Briefing language example 14:36: Abba, meaning “Father”; “Mark places the Aramaic address beside its Greek equivalent in Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane”
findings.problem: The briefing supports only the meaning “Father,” not the child-language or familial-register claims.

findings.guideText: a writer inventing the scene would probably have tidied this, and would almost certainly not have made his own sources the men who slept through it.

findings.problem: The guide turns an apologetic inference about invention and sources into near-certainty that the sources do not establish.

findings.guideText: The name means, roughly, 'son of the father' — an irony most readers have noticed.
findings.evidence: Mark 15:7, 11, 15 and bookBriefing (Barabbas's name is not translated or explained in the chapter text or the briefing).
findings.problem: The guide states an Aramaic etymology for Barabbas as fact, which neither the chapter text nor the book briefing supports.

findings.guideText: the thorn crown parodies the radiate crowns on imperial coins
findings.evidence: Mark 15:17 ("weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on him") and bookBriefing (no mention of radiate crowns or imperial coins).
findings.problem: The guide states a specific historical/numismatic claim about imperial coins as fact without support in the chapter text or book briefing.

findings.guideText: Readers in the Roman world who knew what crucifixion was — Mark uses Latin terms and names Simon's sons as if they were known to his community
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: "Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles"; place: "Traditionally Rome. Latin loanwords fit that setting but do not prove it, and Syria is a major alternative"
findings.problem: The guide narrows the audience to the Roman world and presents a debated Rome inference as settled context.

findings.guideText: Golgotha outside the city wall
findings.evidence: Mark 15:22: "They brought him to the place called Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, “The place of a skull.”"
findings.problem: The chapter does not say Golgotha was outside the city wall, and the briefing does not supply that location claim.

findings.guideText: The name means, roughly, 'son of the father'
findings.evidence: Mark 15:7: "There was one called Barabbas, bound with his fellow insurgents"; briefing language examples for 15:34 identify only "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?"
findings.problem: The Barabbas etymology is a linguistic claim that neither the chapter nor the briefing supplies.

findings.guideText: A Roman public execution reserved for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, designed to be slow, exposed, and humiliating. Roman citizens were normally exempt from it.
findings.evidence: Mark 15:24: "Crucifying him, they parted his garments among them"; the briefing gives no crucifixion eligibility or citizen-exemption claim.
findings.problem: These historical claims about crucifixion are stated as fact without support in the chapter or briefing.

findings.guideText: Counted from sunrise: roughly 9 a.m., noon, and 3 p.m.
findings.evidence: Mark 15:25: "It was the third hour"; 15:33-34 refer to "the sixth hour" and "the ninth hour" without a sunrise conversion.
findings.problem: The chapter and briefing do not support the sunrise-based clock conversion.

findings.guideText: A Roman officer commanding around eighty men.
findings.evidence: Mark 15:39: "When the centurion, who stood by opposite him, saw that he cried out like this and breathed his last"
findings.problem: The chapter and briefing do not give the number of men commanded by this centurion.

findings.guideText: his one question is whether Jesus claims to be King of the Jews
findings.evidence: Mark 15:4: "Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer? See how many things they testify against you!”"; 15:9, 15:12 and 15:14 also record Pilate asking questions.
findings.problem: Pilate asks more than one question in the chapter, so this is not his one question.

findings.guideText: A heavy woven veil separating the innermost sanctuary — the Most Holy Place, which only the high priest entered, once a year — from the rest of the temple.
findings.evidence: Mark 15:38: "The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom."
findings.problem: The chapter and briefing do not supply these details about the veil, the Most Holy Place, or annual entry.

findings.guideText: torn from the top to the bottom, which is to say not by human hands
findings.evidence: Mark 15:38: "The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom."
findings.problem: The verse gives the direction of the tear but does not state that no human hands caused it.

findings.guideText: it happens in a building on the other side of the city from Golgotha
findings.evidence: Mark 15:22 names Golgotha only as "The place of a skull"; 15:38 says only "The veil of the temple was torn."
findings.problem: Neither the chapter nor the briefing gives this relative location for the temple and Golgotha.

findings.guideText: Crucified bodies were normally left to hang or thrown into a common grave; that was part of the punishment.
findings.evidence: Mark 15:46: Joseph "laid him in a tomb which had been cut out of a rock. He rolled a stone against the door of the tomb."
findings.problem: The normal-disposal practice is stated as fact but is supported by neither the chapter nor the briefing.

findings.guideText: takes the one who actually led an armed uprising over the one accused of it
findings.evidence: Mark 15:7: "There was one called Barabbas, bound with his fellow insurgents, men who in the insurrection had committed murder."
findings.problem: The verse associates Barabbas with insurgents but does not say he led the uprising.

findings.guideText: while the Galilean pilgrims who lined the road are elsewhere
findings.evidence: Mark 15:11: "But the chief priests stirred up the multitude, that he should release Barabbas to them instead."
findings.problem: The chapter says nothing about where Galilean pilgrims were during this scene.

findings.guideText: purple was the colour of royalty because the dye was ruinously expensive, the thorn crown parodies the radiate crowns on imperial coins
findings.evidence: Mark 15:17: "They clothed him with purple; and weaving a crown of thorns, they put it on him."
findings.problem: Neither the chapter nor the briefing supports the dye-cost or imperial-coin claims.

findings.problem: The hosted text calls it a written superscription and does not say a sign was nailed over his head.

findings.problem: The audience field drops the book briefing's uncertainty ("Likely") and adds an unsupported claim about what readers already knew from preaching.

findings.evidence: bookBriefing.language and bookBriefing.debates[1]
findings.problem: This linguistic claim about the Greek of verse 8 finishing on a conjunction does not appear in the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.problem: The book briefing cites Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Eusebius, and Jerome, but does not mention Syriac, Old Latin, Armenian, or Georgian manuscripts.

findings.guideText: since Mark uses the same word,

findings.problem: The claim that Mark uses the same word in 14:51-52 and 16:5 is a Greek vocabulary claim not supported by the chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, who would have known the risen Jesus story already from preaching before they ever read it here
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenFor: “Likely Greek-speaking readers outside Judea, probably including Gentiles. That is an inference”
findings.problem: The guide drops the briefing’s uncertainty and adds prior knowledge of the resurrection story that the briefing does not state.

findings.guideText: Somewhere in the AD 50s–70s; verses 9-20 are generally dated later than the rest
findings.evidence: Briefing writtenWhen: “Most scholarship places it from the mid-AD 60s to shortly after 70, though earlier dates are defended.”
findings.problem: The guide changes the briefing’s dating range and adds a separate dating claim for verses 9-20 that the briefing does not give.

findings.guideText: The Greek of verse 8 finishes on a conjunction, which is an unusual way to end a sentence, let alone a book
findings.evidence: Briefing debate on the ending says Sinaiticus and Vaticanus “stop at 16:8, with the women fleeing in silence” and gives no claim about the Greek final word being a conjunction.
findings.problem: This Greek claim is stated as fact but is not supported by the hosted chapter text or the book briefing.

findings.guideText: So do the oldest Syriac, an old Latin manuscript, and the earliest Armenian and Georgian versions.
findings.evidence: Briefing debate grounds: “The two oldest complete Greek Bibles — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both 4th century — stop at 16:8. Eusebius and Jerome both report that the accurate copies available to them ended there.”
findings.problem: The Syriac, Latin, Armenian, and Georgian manuscript claims are not supported by the supplied briefing.

findings.guideText: Then read 9-20 knowing what they are: an early and widely received summary of appearances recorded elsewhere, added by a hand other than the one that wrote the rest.
findings.evidence: Briefing debate position: “The longer ending, 16:9-20, belongs” because “It is in the vast majority of surviving manuscripts and was quoted as scripture by the 2nd century” and is canonical in Catholic and Orthodox tradition.
findings.problem: The guide presents one side of a live textual debate as settled fact instead of preserving the disagreement named in the briefing.

findings.guideText: Variants: several different endings survive in the manuscript tradition — a shorter one, this longer one, both together, and this one with an extra insertion — which is the pattern you get when copyists are trying to solve a problem, not when they are transmitting an original.
findings.evidence: Briefing debate on the ending supports only that Sinaiticus and Vaticanus stop at 16:8 and that verses 9-20 are in most manuscripts and quoted by the 2nd century.
findings.problem: The detailed list of ending variants and the conclusion about copyists’ motives are not supported by the supplied briefing.

findings.guideText: And Paul's list of resurrection witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 is earlier than any of the gospels.

findings.problem: This dating claim is stated as fact without support in the chapter text or briefing.

findings.guideText: In first-century Jewish and Roman society, a woman's testimony carried little weight and was in some legal settings not accepted at all.

findings.problem: This historical and legal claim is stated as fact but is unsupported by the grounding bundle.

findings.problem: The guide forces one historical explanation for the women’s presence instead of presenting it as a debated inference.

findings.problem: The underlying Greek word claim is not supported by the supplied briefing.

findings.guideText: the last human action in Mark's gospel is a command disobeyed out of fear
findings.evidence: Mark 16:10: “She went and told those who had been with him”; Mark 16:20: “They went out and preached everywhere”
findings.problem: As written, this contradicts the hosted chapter, which continues beyond verse 8 with later human actions.

findings.guideText: A small number of groups have read it as a command and handled venomous snakes in worship, with fatalities; the overwhelming majority of Christian traditions read it as a description of protection in the course of the mission, not a practice to seek out.
findings.evidence: Mark 16:17-18 lists signs accompanying believers; neither those verses nor the briefing discusses snake-handling groups, fatalities, or the view of the overwhelming majority of traditions.
findings.problem: These historical and tradition-wide claims are stated as fact without support in the grounding bundle.
